title: "Sum coding"

Treatment coding makes one observed category the reference. [**Sum coding**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=133) instead makes the intercept the unweighted mean of the fitted category means at the numeric predictor reference values.

The [design matrix](design-matrices.qmd) turns each category into coefficient multipliers. For three levels, sum coding uses two contrast columns. Its intercept gives the three coded source categories equal weight, without claiming to represent a population-weighted lexical mean.

The claim about the intercept must follow from the contrast matrix rather than the label “sum coding.” Reconstructing the three MALD category means then checks whether the fitted values remain unchanged under treatment coding.

Let the three adjusted category means be $\mu_N$, $\mu_V$, and $\mu_A$. Treatment coding uses one of these means as its intercept and describes the others through differences from that reference. Sum coding instead places the intercept at $(\mu_N+\mu_V+\mu_A)/3$ and describes category deviations around that value. The predictions have not moved. We have changed the coordinates used to recover them, which we verify with the observed MALD categories below.

## Different coordinates for the same MALD means

For three levels, R's sum-coding matrix is

$$
\begin{array}{c|rr}
&S_1&S_2\\\hline
\text{noun}&1&0\\
\text{verb}&0&1\\
\text{adjective}&-1&-1
\end{array}.
$$

The category-specific fitted means at centered numeric predictors are

$$
\mu_N=\beta_0+\beta_1,
\qquad
\mu_V=\beta_0+\beta_2,
\qquad
\mu_A=\beta_0-\beta_1-\beta_2.
$$

Averaging them gives

$$
\frac{\mu_N+\mu_V+\mu_A}{3}=\beta_0.
$$

If the observed category counts are $n_N$, $n_V$, and $n_A$, the observation-weighted fitted mean is

$$
\frac{n_N\mu_N+n_V\mu_V+n_A\mu_A}{n_N+n_V+n_A}.
$$

This quantity need not equal $(\mu_N+\mu_V+\mu_A)/3$ when the category counts differ. Sum coding targets the unweighted category reference, not the observation-weighted reference.

If the observed category counts differ, the mean weighted by observations need not equal the equally weighted category mean. The sum coding intercept gives each fitted category mean one third of the weight. Thus the word *mean* is incomplete until we say which units receive equal weight.

## Verifying fitted-value invariance

```{r}
#| label: compare-mald-treatment-and-sum-coding
mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-items.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mald$log_frequency_c <-
  mald$log_frequency_subtlex - mean(mald$log_frequency_subtlex)
mald$log_duration_c <- mald$log_duration - mean(mald$log_duration)
mald$n_phones_c <- mald$n_phones - mean(mald$n_phones)
major_pos <- subset(
  mald,
  part_of_speech %in% c("Noun", "Verb", "Adjective")
)

treatment_data <- major_pos
treatment_data$part_of_speech <- factor(
  treatment_data$part_of_speech,
  levels = c("Noun", "Verb", "Adjective")
)
contrasts(treatment_data$part_of_speech) <- contr.treatment(3)

sum_data <- major_pos
sum_data$part_of_speech <- factor(
  sum_data$part_of_speech,
  levels = c("Noun", "Verb", "Adjective")
)
contrasts(sum_data$part_of_speech) <- contr.sum(3)

formula <- mean_log_rt ~ part_of_speech + log_frequency_c +
  log_duration_c + n_phones_c
fit_treatment <- lm(formula, data = treatment_data)
fit_sum <- lm(formula, data = sum_data)
maximum_fit_difference <- max(abs(
  fitted(fit_treatment) - fitted(fit_sum)
))

stopifnot(maximum_fit_difference < 1e-10)

contrasts(sum_data$part_of_speech)
rbind(treatment = coef(fit_treatment), sum = coef(fit_sum))
```

The largest difference between fitted values is `r format(maximum_fit_difference, scientific = TRUE, digits = 2)`. A **basis** is a set of independent columns that can generate every fitted category pattern under consideration. Treatment and sum coding use different bases for the same set of patterns, so their coefficients differ while their column spaces and fitted item means agree.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mald-sum-coding-means
#| fig-cap: "Observed MALD item summaries and fitted category means. Recoding changes coefficients, not these fitted means."
library(ggplot2)

prediction_data <- data.frame(
  part_of_speech = factor(
    levels(treatment_data$part_of_speech),
    levels = levels(treatment_data$part_of_speech)
  ),
  log_frequency_c = 0,
  log_duration_c = 0,
  n_phones_c = 0
)
prediction_data$fit <- predict(fit_treatment, newdata = prediction_data)
prediction_data$observed_items <- as.integer(
  table(treatment_data$part_of_speech)[as.character(prediction_data$part_of_speech)]
)

prediction_data[, c("part_of_speech", "observed_items", "fit")]

point_opacity <- 0.08
ggplot(treatment_data, aes(part_of_speech, mean_log_rt)) +
  geom_jitter(color = "grey70", alpha = point_opacity, width = 0.16, height = 0, size = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = prediction_data, aes(y = fit), color = "#2C6E9B", size = 2) +
  labs(
    x = "Frequency-dominant part of speech",
    y = "Mean log lexical-decision time"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The table reports the observed number of word items and the adjusted fitted mean for each recorded category. The sum-coded intercept gives equal weight to those three fitted means even though the observed category counts differ. That distinction should be named whenever the categories are unbalanced.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Why does the sum-coded intercept equal an unweighted category mean?
2. Why can coefficients change while fitted values do not?
3. Does the intercept weight categories by their observed sample sizes?
4. What property of the design matrix is invariant under a full-rank recoding?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The three coded category deviations cancel, leaving the intercept equal to $(\mu_N+\mu_V+\mu_A)/3$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. A full-rank recoding changes the basis used to name coefficients while preserving the same design-matrix column space. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. No. The sum-coded intercept gives each fitted category mean weight one third, regardless of the observed number of items in that category. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The column space, and thus the projection onto fitted values, is invariant. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
